analysis.title: Monetary Policy Navigator: October MPM preview: BoJ expected to indicate that inflation is "at level consistent with" 2% target
key_insights: MUMSS forecasts the BoJ will hold the policy rate at 1.25% at the October 29-30 meeting, after hikes in June and September. With a little over a month since the September hike and no new upside inflation risks, the Bank is expected to wait and see.
MUMSS expects an 8-1 vote, with Hajime Takata, the most hawkish board member, dissenting in favor of back-to-back hikes.

In the Outlook Report the BoJ is expected to conclude that underlying inflation is at a level generally consistent with the 2% target. That would acknowledge that the target set in the January 2013 Joint Statement has been achieved, about 13 years later.

The BoJ is expected to shift from focusing on downside inflation risks to monitoring risks in both directions. At the October 16 post-G20 press conference Governor Ueda said 'We cannot tolerate any further rise [in underlying inflation],' stronger language than before.
MUMSS notes consecutive or larger hikes could become possible depending on circumstances, so the BoJ's inflation assessment warrants closer attention than before.
MUMSS is watching whether the Takaichi administration, which so far only says Japan is 'not in deflation', declares an end to deflation.
MUMSS expects the BoJ to raise its real GDP growth forecasts for FY26 and FY27 from the July projections of +0.6% and +0.8%. It expects risks to activity to stay 'generally balanced'.

FY26 and FY27 inflation forecasts may be revised slightly higher on rising costs and the recent rebound in crude oil. MUMSS expects the BoJ to reaffirm that CPI risks are 'skewed to the upside' and that underlying inflation could deviate above 2%. The BoJ's analysis finds firms passing on costs faster than before.
The BoJ's projections appear not to include the effect of the consumption tax cut under deliberation in the Diet.

Policy guidance is likely to change only in wording: 'given that underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2%' would be replaced by something like 'is at a level generally consistent with the 2% inflation target'. The 'financial conditions have been accommodative' language is expected to stay.

Evidence of a rate-hike drag on lending is thin. The September Tankan showed little change in the DIs for corporate financial positions and bank lending attitudes, and the corporate loan demand DI in the October Senior Loan Officer survey rose from the previous survey.
Ueda said on September 18 that long and super-long interest rates have become considerably more restrictive, while the lending and asset-market channels remain somewhat accommodative.

At the press conference Ueda is likely to avoid specifying the timing of the next hike. Last week markets moved to risk-off (equities down, yen stronger, bonds rallied), so he may say market sentiment will factor into the pace of future hikes.
MUMSS expects hikes to 1.50% in December 2026 (meeting December 17-18) and to 1.75% in April 2027 (April 27-28), completing the adjustment of monetary accommodation.

A three-month spacing would point to a March 17-18 hike, but MUMSS thinks the BoJ would avoid hiking just before fiscal year-end because of deposit and mortgage rate sensitivity. April also brings the first FY29 forecasts. A consumption tax cut taking effect in April 2027 adds uncertainty to March purchases and retail prices.

Terminal-rate upside risk: demand and supply shocks lift underlying inflation and the BoJ keeps hiking after real rates turn positive. Downside risk: the BoJ stops at 1.25% or 1.50%, or pauses, if prolonged global market instability raises downside risks to activity.

risk_factors: Upside inflation risk: firms are passing on costs faster, and the recent rebound in crude oil lifts costs.
Prolonged global financial market instability, equities and exchange rates, could stop BoJ tightening at 1.25% or 1.50%.
Demand and supply shocks could push underlying inflation higher and lead the BoJ to keep hiking after real rates turn positive.
Uncertainty over consumption and retail prices around the April 2027 consumption tax cut.
vol_and_positioning: Last week markets moved into risk-off: equities fell, the yen strengthened and bonds rallied.
geopolitical: The BoJ's September guidance cited the situation in the Middle East as a risk to the outlook for activity and prices.
The Takaichi administration has so far said only that Japan is 'not in deflation'.
The Diet is deliberating a consumption tax cut, expected to take effect in April 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Demand and supply shocks lift underlying inflation and the BoJ keeps raising rates after real rates turn positive, above the 1.75% base case.
tension_points.bear_case: Prolonged instability in global financial markets raises downside risks to activity, and the BoJ stops tightening at 1.25% or 1.50% or pauses.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A prolonged global equity and exchange-rate disruption would undercut the December and April hike path.

theme_stances.key_argument: Underlying inflation is consistent with 2% and upside risks persist, so the BoJ keeps hiking to 1.50% in December and 1.75% in April.
theme_stances.evidence: we anticipate additional rate hikes in December 2026 and April 2027
